content: Topical gentamicin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat specific bacterial skin infections, such as impetigo or folliculitis. It is also prescribed for infections associated with certain skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis, as well as for infected burns, sores, or wounds. However, its effectiveness may vary depending on the bacteria causing the infection, as some bacteria may have developed resistance to gentamicin. Your healthcare provider may also recommend it for other conditions based on your specific needs. How Topical Gentamicin Works Topical gentamicin works by killing certain types of bacteria. It achieves this by preventing the bacteria from producing proteins essential for their survival and growth. Dosage Forms Topical gentamicin is available in the following forms: 1% topical cream 1% topical ointment Storage Instructions Store topical gentamicin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). How to Use Topical gentamicin is intended for application on the skin only. It should not be applied to the eyes. If you are using it to treat impetigo, remove any crusts from the affected area before applying the medication. Always use the medication exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Precautions Do not use topical gentamicin unless prescribed by a healthcare provider. Avoid sharing this medication with others, even if they have similar symptoms, as it may harm them. Keep the medication out of reach of children. Inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, supplements, or herbal products you are using. This helps them determine if topical gentamicin is appropriate for you. Who Should Not Use Topical Gentamicin? Individuals allergic to gentamicin or any ingredients in the specific product should not use it. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the product. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding It is not known whether topical gentamicin affects pregnancy or harms an unborn baby. Inform your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It is also unclear if topical gentamicin passes into breast milk. Discuss breastfeeding with your healthcare provider before using this medication. Drug Interactions There are no known interactions between topical gentamicin and foods, drinks, or other medications. However, it is unknown if alcohol consumption affects the medication. Missed Dose If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not use double or extra doses. Completing the full prescribed course is essential, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Overdose If you or someone else uses too much topical gentamicin, seek medical help immediately. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Common Side Effects The most common side effects include: Skin redness Skin itching Skin irritation If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here. Contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. Serious Side Effects Although rare, serious allergic reactions can occur. Stop using topical gentamicin and seek immediate medical attention if you experience: Breathing problems or wheezing Rapid heartbeat Fever or general unwellness Swollen lymph nodes Swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat Difficulty swallowing or throat tightness Itching, skin rash, or hives Nausea or vomiting Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting Stomach cramps Joint pain Risk of Secondary Infections Using topical gentamicin may lead to infections caused by other types of germs, such as fungi. If you suspect a secondary infection, consult your healthcare provider. By following these guidelines and consulting your healthcare provider as needed, you can use topical gentamicin safely and effectively.
